source: Ash, Cushen & Wiley (2009) Obstacles in investigating the role of restructuring in insightful problem solving
finding: Restructuring theories rest on three assumptions that need direct tests: the problem is represented wrongly at first (representational difficulty), the representation then changes (representational change), and the solution comes in a jump (discontinuity). The paper lists method obstacles and gives advice for future studies.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Journal of Problem Solving 2(2), 6-41.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; the full PDF sat behind a bot wall. The detail of each obstacle is not recorded here.
agent_relevance: The S6 test set cannot assume that a task 'is' an insight task. Each item needs evidence of a wrong first representation, a change, and a jump.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) citing Ash et al. (2009) on measurement difficulty
finding: Webb et al. say the methodological challenges of objectively measuring a subjective phenomenon such as insight are well known, and cite Oellinger & Knoblich 2009 and Ash et al. 2009.
numbers: n/a
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the feeling of insight as a ground-truth label.

source: Ash & Wiley (2006) The nature of restructuring in insight: an individual-differences approach
finding: Working-memory span predicted success on insight problems that allow a large faulty search space, but not on matched problems that isolate the restructuring phase. The authors read this as support for automatic redistribution of activation in restructuring, not controlled search.
numbers: 207 students recruited; 3 dropped for incomplete data, 1 for solution times over the limit; N=203 with WM data (RSPAN M=66%, OSPAN M=66%, r=.64). Regression on number solved: WMSPAN beta=.27, p<.01, block R2=.08; adding a WMSPAN x problem-type interaction gave R2 change .046, F(1,111)=5.81, p<.05. Solve time: WMSPAN beta=-.22, p<.05 for the full-search problem set; no WM effect on restructuring-isolating problems.
quote: increased ability to control attention (as measured by WM span tasks) predicts an individual's ability to successfully solve problems that involve both the initial search phase and the restructuring phase
limits: Correlational. Individual differences in WM only. The two problem sets (full-search vs constrained) may differ in more than search space. One lab, student sample.
agent_relevance: A matched-pair design (same surface, search space shrunk) is a way to build S6 items that isolate restructuring from search. Do not assume more attention-like effort helps the restructuring step itself.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types
finding: Three experiments used classic insight problems, non-insight problems and Compound Remote Associates (CRAs), with continuous ratings of Aha, confidence, surprise, impasse and pleasure. For insight problems and CRAs, correct solutions carried stronger insight feeling than wrong ones. The authors argue the task label does not fix whether insight happens.
numbers: Exp 1: 193 Melbourne students (118 female), 9 removed for errors on over 20% of tasks. Exp 1a (ESL students filtered): task type on accuracy F(2,158)=33.98, eta2=.30; non-insight beat insight by 0.15 and CRA by 0.23; insight beat CRA by 0.08. Accuracy-Aha correlation: insight problems r=.40, CRAs r=.40, non-insight problems r=.24 (p=.04, weak) where Exp 1 found none.
quote: classic insight and non-insight problems alike can be solved with both insight and analysis
limits: Pattern shifted between Exp 1 and 1a (insight vs CRA Aha difference vanished after ESL filtering). CRAs are a hybrid. Later experiments' sample sizes not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Aha-accuracy links are task-dependent and unstable. A test set for S6 should label items by solver behaviour, not by puzzle family.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types - surprise
finding: Surprise behaved oddly in Exp 1a: it related negatively to accuracy yet positively (weak to moderate) to Aha, so it may separate Aha from plain pleasure and confidence.
numbers: Exp 1a: negative surprise-accuracy link, weak-to-moderate positive surprise-Aha link (exact r not copied).
limits: One dataset. Danek & Wiley (2017) later found Surprise barely tied to Aha (r=.07) and said Webb et al. had r from .29 to .48.
agent_relevance: If an agent logs a confidence-jump signal, keep it separate from a surprise signal.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types - Metcalfe 1986 caveat
finding: The paper notes Metcalfe (1986) found people often give an inelegant but plausible wrong answer with high feeling of warmth. Poincare (1913) had already noted Aha can accompany wrong ideas. Salvi et al. (2016) found Aha predicts accuracy, but mostly on non-classic problems (CRAs, rebus, anagrams).
numbers: n/a (narrative).
limits: Secondary report; Metcalfe and Salvi papers not opened.
agent_relevance: A felt 'got it' is not proof of a right answer. Supports G3 and G5: a pass must come from a check, not a feeling.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types - task definition
finding: Insight definitions vary on three dimensions: process, task and phenomenology (Oellinger & Knoblich 2009). The four-coin weighing task, called non-insight, can still give Aha to a naive solver. The water-lily problem works as an insight task only if the solver first fixates on '60' and 'half'.
numbers: Water lilies: answer 59; common wrong answer 30. Four-coin task: two weighings.
limits: Argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Insight status belongs to the solver-problem pair. S6 items need a manipulation check that the wrong representation was adopted (for example a logged wrong first move).

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions
finding: False insights exist. With 35 magic-trick problems, wrong solutions often got strong Aha ratings. Aha has several parts; Pleasure, Suddenness and Certainty were the key ones.
numbers: N=70, 35 tricks, 2450 trials; 603 timeouts and 69 missing, leaving 1778 solutions: 36.8% correct (654), 63.2% wrong (1124). Aha: correct M=66.50 SD=18.42 vs wrong M=52.34 SD=18.78, t(69)=10.21. 417 of 1124 wrong solutions (37%) had Aha above the mean for correct ones. Solve time: correct 35.81 s vs wrong 42.46 s, t(1776)=6.26. Aha vs Surprise r=.07; vs Pleasure r=.66; vs Certainty r=.58.
quote: These results cast some doubt on the assumption that the occurrence of an Aha! experience can serve as a definitive signal that a true insight has taken place.
limits: One task family (magic tricks). Self report. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Felt certainty on a fast answer is a weak label; fast wrong answers also feel good. Use speed plus feeling only as a trigger to verify (G1), never as acceptance.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions - time as cue
finding: Solve time predicted Aha: faster solutions got higher Aha. Fast wrong answers may inflate Aha because speed is used as a cue; slow wrong answers got low Aha.
numbers: Mixed model: solution time t=4.03, p<.01; correctness t=-3.36, p<.01; interaction t=1.58, p<.12 (not significant).
limits: Correlational; cue use is inferred.
agent_relevance: Fast, confident, wrong answers are a failure mode. A 'too easy, check it' rule fits better than 'trust the quick insight'.

source: Wiley & Danek (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments (Journal of Intelligence 14(9))
finding: Aha ratings are better read as 'Judgments of Aha' (JOAs), inferred from cues such as fluency and correctness. They were highest for correct solutions that began with a correct first move, not for solutions that needed a changed representation.
numbers: N=377 students, 4 spatial object-move puzzles (2 matchstick arithmetic, triangle of coins, matchstick fish). 1508 trials: 223 dropped as seen before, 120 missing; 1164 analysed. Aha-correctness effect F(1,1091)=112.17, p<.001, partial R2=.09, 95% CI [.06,.12], f2=.099. Three-level index (wrong / correct after wrong first move / correct after correct first move) F(2,1079)=71.48, partial R2=.11, f2=.126. Coder kappa .94 for first-move scoring.
quote: Aha! experiences are more closely tied to achieving correct solutions than to restructuring processes.
limits: Spatial puzzles, one US university. Correct-after-wrong-first-move was rare. Matchstick problems showed weaker effects.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for S6: Aha is tied to being right, not to having restructured. Score restructuring by trace evidence (a wrong first move, then a changed one), not by a feeling label.

source: Wiley & Danek (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments (Journal of Intelligence 14(9)) - mixed matchstick replications
finding: For matchstick arithmetic, the Aha-correctness link has mixed support across labs: present in Kizilirmak et al. 2021, absent in Strickland et al. 2022. Verbal tasks show it robustly; non-verbal tasks robustly only for magic tricks (before this study).
numbers: Fish and Triangle puzzles: effect for both kinds of correct solution. Matchstick puzzles: effect only for correct-after-correct-first-move; no difference between correct-after-revision and wrong.
limits: Cited studies not opened; only the 2026 paper's account.
agent_relevance: Expect task-family variance. Report S6 results per family, never pooled.

source: Wiley & Danek (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments (Journal of Intelligence 14(9)) - spread of Aha
finding: Aha reports now appear in polysemy resolution, garden-path sentences, divergent thinking and conceptual change, which may involve different restructuring kinds.
numbers: Citations only (Smith 2025; Dygert & Jarosz 2026; Smith 2026; Chesebrough 2023).
limits: Secondary account.
agent_relevance: Wide use of the Aha label makes it a poor sole marker of an 'insight task'.

source: Smith et al. (2026) Comparing Aha! moments in problem solving and generative ideation (Journal of Intelligence 14(8))
finding: Using a two-step report (Aha yes/no, then strength), Aha strength did not differ between CRA/Polysemous Associates solutions and category-generation responses. In generation, later responses were more likely to be Aha responses, with longer pauses and higher novelty.
numbers: 77 students enrolled; 8 excluded for incomplete data, 5 excluded for reporting every response as Aha. No Aha-strength difference between task types or between ad hoc and taxonomic categories.
quote: later responses were increasingly likely to be aha! responses
limits: Verbal tasks. Excluding 'always Aha' responders shows a response-style problem in self report. Exact test statistics not recorded.
agent_relevance: A 'late idea feels special' effect comes from retrieval dynamics, not reframing. Do not read an agent's late-idea confidence as insight.

source: Macchi, Poli & Caravona (2025) Dissociable effects of verbalization on solving insight and non-insight problems
finding: Thinking aloud hurt the insight problem (Deer) and helped the non-insight problem (cryptarithmetic). This fits a process split, against the pure business-as-usual view.
numbers: Deer insight problem: 13% solved while verbalizing vs 57% silent. Cryptarithmetic: 80% solved verbalizing vs 30% silent. 10-minute limit; Cox hazard model.
limits: One insight and one non-insight problem. Cell sizes not copied. Item-specific.
agent_relevance: Forcing a written chain at an insight-type step may cost accuracy, while it helps stepwise steps. Test by item type before forcing chains of thought at S6.

source: Macchi, Poli & Caravona (2025) Dissociable effects of verbalization on solving insight and non-insight problems - camps and earlier verbalization work
finding: Fleck & Weisberg 2013: writing thoughts lowered insight success. Special-process side cites Knoblich 1999/2001, Kershaw & Ohlsson 2004, Jung-Beeman 2004; business-as-usual side cites Perkins 1981, Chronicle 2004, Fleck & Weisberg 2004/2013, Danek 2016, Weisberg 2015. A third view is unconscious analytic thought.
numbers: n/a (narrative).
limits: Secondary; earlier papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The field has no agreed marker of insight, which is the measurement problem itself.

source: Salmon-Mordekovich & Leikin (2023) Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite 'as usual'
finding: Four problem types (verbal insight, spatial insight, verbal non-insight, spatial non-insight) under silence, articulatory suppression and a non-verbal attention load. Insight problems were solved mostly by analytic routes (analogical and convergent thinking) unaffected by the secondary tasks. A rare exceptional route shows traits of the special-process account.
numbers: N=115 undergraduates (92 women, mean age 26.25), Hebrew speakers; planned with G*Power (f=.25, alpha .01, power .95 for RM-MANOVA).
quote: The results indicate a typical, analytic solution method consistent with the business-as-usual theory.
limits: Single language and lab; the 'exceptional' route is an interpretation. Per-condition accuracy not copied.
agent_relevance: A test set for S6 will mix typical analytic solves and rare jumps. Plan to measure both.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704v2)
finding: A renewable riddle benchmark built to need a representational shift, not recall. 38 models scored far below humans. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones. Model size did not predict accuracy; release date did.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human subset. Non-reasoning avg 7.60% (n=16), reasoning avg 17.59% (n=19), human 52.9% (pilot n=126). Over all 201 items: 9.42% vs 19.25%; odds ratio 2.29, 95% CI [1.99, 2.64]; Welch t(24.093)=2.976, p=.00655, diff 9.804 pp, d=0.946. Parameter size vs accuracy Pearson r=-0.017 (p=.919, n=38); release date Spearman rho=.402 (p=.0123). Search-augmented models near human; GPT-5 the exception among retrieval-free models; a harder set is planned where GPT-5 scores 33%.
quote: models sometimes generated correct candidates but failed to endorse them
limits: Japanese wordplay. Human baseline is a pilot with bimodal scores. Thought-log analysis is qualitative and hypothesis-generating.
agent_relevance: A cheap, rotatable item source for S6 tests, and evidence that surface-fluent models fail the shift step.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704v2) - verification failure and false Aha
finding: Logs show 'verification failure': the model reaches the right answer, does not recognise it and moves on (Grok-4, Claude Opus 4). Logs also show 'false Aha': an Aha-like utterance followed by a wrong answer. Aha-like cases that led to the correct answer were rare.
numbers: Cases named by item (Grok-4 Q18, Q26, Q31, Q198; Claude-opus-4 Q35, Q135, Q179). Thought language: DeepSeek-R1-0528 100% Japanese (199/199); Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 94% English; Grok-4 57.2% Japanese.
limits: Qualitative, small case counts, no inter-rater statistics seen.
agent_relevance: A recognition gap: the model may generate the answer but lack a check that confirms it. Fits G3 and G6: keep candidates and verify with code or a held-out check, not the model's feeling.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704v2) - human contrast
finding: The authors say verification failures are rare in humans, who usually notice a correct answer once it appears, and cite human false Aha (Danek & Wiley 2017) as real but less frequent.
numbers: Authors' judgement, not a measured human rate.
limits: No human think-aloud data collected.
agent_relevance: Humans track correctness through a feeling of rightness that current models lack. A code-side checker has to replace that signal.

source: D'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models (arXiv 2601.00514v2)
finding: Mid-trace 'Aha' shifts ('Wait, let's re-evaluate') are rare, do not grow with RL training, and seldom raise accuracy. Their effect depends on model uncertainty. Forcing an extrinsic shift under high entropy does raise accuracy.
numbers: Over 1M traces; GRPO-tuned Qwen2.5 and Llama; three domains (Math, Xwords, RHour). Shifts about 7.6% of samples in one setting; 6.31% pooled. Shifted traces 2.57% correct vs 16.44% for non-shifted. A formal detector fires on 1.79% of samples. Entropy buckets: top 20% vs bottom 80% within domain.
quote: reasoning shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with training, and seldom improve accuracy
limits: Small open models, not frontier reasoning models. Rates depend strongly on the detector (about 1% to 7%).
agent_relevance: Supports G1: doubt works when triggered by a signal such as high entropy, not by the model's own pivot talk. Test an entropy or disagreement trigger.

source: D'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models (arXiv 2601.00514v2) - raw effects by entropy
finding: Raw effect of a shift on accuracy was strongly negative in both entropy buckets in the printed tables (about -22.5 to -22.9 percentage points), yet extrinsic shifts under high entropy raised accuracy.
numbers: Raw effects printed: -22.48 pp (high entropy), -22.88 to -22.90 pp (low entropy).
limits: Read from extracted table text; row labels not verified one by one.
agent_relevance: Natural shifts mark trouble; they are not a repair. Inserted shifts under uncertainty are.

source: Latif et al. (2024) Can OpenAI o1 outperform humans in higher-order cognitive thinking? (arXiv 2412.05753)
finding: Not an insight study. o1-preview beat human means on critical thinking, systematic thinking, data literacy, creative originality, logic and science reasoning. One riddle paper cites it for insight tasks, which the abstract does not show.
numbers: Ennis-Weir 24.33 vs undergraduate 13.8 and postgraduate 18.39; Lake Urmia 46.1 vs 20.08; originality 2.98 vs 1.74; LogiQA 90% vs 86%; TOSLS 0.99 vs 0.85.
limits: Abstract page only; no candle or nine-dot task in it. The claim that LLMs beat humans on classic insight tasks is not supported by what I read.
agent_relevance: Classic puzzles are probably memorised. Use fresh, rotated items such as NazoNazo.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) and Weisberg (1995) as described by Webb et al. (2016)
finding: Webb et al. say the use of insight and non-insight problem sets stems largely from these two papers, whose authors themselves noted the distinction is vague.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Secondary. Originals not opened.
agent_relevance: The task-based split of insight vs non-insight was never firmly defined; S6 should not inherit it.

source: Bowden et al. (2005) New approaches to demystifying insight (as cited by Webb et al. 2016)
finding: Cited as part of a push to study insight phenomenology with self report in lab studies (also Danek et al. 2014b).
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Secondary.
agent_relevance: Self report is the common method; its validity is what the 2016-2026 papers challenge.

source: Wiley & Danek (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments - data loss
finding: Puzzle contamination and timeouts remove many trials: people who had seen a problem before were excluded, as were missed deadlines.
numbers: Of 1508 trials, 223 (14.8%) excluded as seen before and 120 (8.0%) missing; 89 trials ran 180-240 s past the 180 s timer because of server lag and were kept.
limits: Human lab data; the rate depends on how famous the puzzle is.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, every well-known puzzle is a seen-before item. S6 needs novel items and a contamination check.
